```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
library(mortensor)
```

## Data

### How do I bring my own data in?

`mt_data()` takes long data frames, one row per cell, with a column for
deaths, exposures or population and columns for age, period and strata.
Ages can be single years, labels such as `"<1"`, `"01-04"`, `"85-89"`,
`"90+"`, `"85 and over"`, or two columns with lower and upper bounds:

```{r}
parse_age_labels(c("<1", "01-04", "85-89", "90+", "85 and over"))
d <- data.frame(region = "A", year = 2019, age = c("85-89", "90+"), deaths = c(120, 210),
                exposure = c(2500, 1400))
mt_data(deaths = d, exposure = d, by = "region")
```

Deaths and exposures may come at different resolutions (for example deaths
in 5-year groups, exposures by single year of age). Tables in wide format,
with one value column per sex or cause, are read by listing the columns
(`value = list(deaths = c(female = "Female", male = "Male"))`). Values
given as text with symbols for suppressed or missing cells (`"."`, `"x"`,
`"-"`) are recognised; other symbols are declared with `missing` and
`zero`. Readers exist for Human Mortality Database tables (`mt_from_hmd()`,
`mt_read_hmd()`), GENESIS and GBE-Bund exports from Destatis
(`mt_read_genesis()`, `mt_read_gbe()`), `StMoMoData` and `demogdata`
objects (`as_mt_data()`).

### I have populations on 31 December, not exposures. What now?

Add them with `mt_add_population()` and convert them with
`mt_as_exposure()`: `type = "jan1"` takes the mean of the populations at
the start of two consecutive years (a population on 31 December is the
population on 1 January of the next year), `type = "midyear"` uses
mid-year populations as they are. Exposures are the denominator of the
rates, so this step matters for the level of every forecast.

### What does `mt_validate()` check?

Cells with zero exposure, deaths without exposure, death rates above one
below age 100, grid cells without observations, and, with a hierarchy,
whether totals equal the sums of their parts (deaths and exposures add up over regions or sexes; rates add up over
causes, `mt_hierarchy(cause = "all", additive = "rates")`).

## Granularity and ungrouping

### Should I model single years of age or the age groups of my data?

Model at the resolution the question needs. Life expectancy, probabilities
of dying and age-standardised rates can be computed from 5-year groups (the
life table uses the interval widths). Single years are needed when results
are reported by single year, when a model needs them (cohort models such as
APC need equal age and period steps), or when data at different
resolutions are combined. Backtests always score against the deaths at
their observed resolution, so ungrouping errors count against the model,
and `mt_backtest()` with and without `step_ungroup()` answers the question
for your data.

### Which ungrouping method should I use?

The penalized composite link model (`mt_ungroup()`, default) ungroups
deaths as rates with the exposures as offset and keeps group totals
exactly. On England & Wales (HMD) data grouped into 5-year groups its median
absolute error of single-year log rates was 0.015 at ages 30-89 and 0.024 at
90-100, close to the Poisson noise of the observed rates. The spline
methods (`"hyman_kannisto"`, `"natural_gompertz"`, `"gam"`) were as
accurate below 90, less accurate in the open interval, and 5 to 10 times
faster. See "Data at different granularities".

### Can I split the open interval 90+ into single years?

Only from assumptions: the data say nothing about the age pattern inside
the interval. `mt_ungroup()` warns when it extrapolates. Prefer a grid
whose open interval starts where the data's does, or data with a higher
open age (for example exposures to 100+ with deaths to 90+, where the
exposures carry the age pattern).

## Models and uncertainty

### Which model should I use?

There is no single best model. Rolling-origin backtests on your own data
(`mt_backtest()`) are the way to choose, ideally with horizons like the
ones you will report. In the vignettes:

* Lee-Carter and Li-Lee were the most accurate on the ONS deprivation data
  over 5 years; Li-Lee keeps the strata from diverging.
* The random walk with drift is a strong benchmark on noisy or short series.
* Ensembles of Lee-Carter and the random walk had the best calibrated 95%
  intervals on real data.
* Bayesian age-period-cohort models (`apc_bayes()`) suit data with cohort
  effects and small counts.

### Why are my 95% intervals too narrow (or too wide)?

Intervals of most models describe the uncertainty of their own
assumptions, for example a constant drift. On real data, changes of trend
add uncertainty that these assumptions leave out, so intervals tend to be
too narrow over 5 to 10 years: in backtests on HMD and ONS data the 95%
coverage of Lee-Carter was 0.70 to 0.84. The plain random walk is wider,
because year-to-year changes of observed rates contain observation noise
twice; that extra width happened to give good 95% coverage on real data.
`rwd(observation_noise = TRUE)` removes the double counting and is sharper
(lower CRPS), with intervals that were too narrow on real data. Mixtures of
models (`mt_ensemble()`) widen the intervals where the models disagree.
Check calibration with `mt_backtest()` and `mt_plot_coverage()`.

### What is the difference between predictive draws and forecast rates?

`mt_forecast()` returns draws of the smooth death rates by default.
`predictive = TRUE` adds the variation of observed rates around them
(extra-Poisson and Poisson noise given the exposures), which is what an
observed future rate will show. Backtests use predictive draws because they
are compared with observed rates. For life expectancy and other summaries
of the underlying mortality, use the default draws.

### How do I handle small populations and zero deaths?

Models that take logs of observed rates (the random walk, the SVD
version of Lee-Carter, Li-Lee) replace zero deaths by 0.5, which is
harmless for a few cells and distorting for many; the Poisson Lee-Carter
handles zeros directly. With many small cells:

* model at a coarser resolution (age groups instead of single years);
* pool information across strata, for example `li_lee(common_by = "sex")`
  for regions or deprivation groups, or `apc_bayes()` with its smoothing
  priors;
* combine rare causes of death into larger groups (see `ons_cause_groups`).

### How should I treat the COVID-19 years?

Either end the training data in 2019 (as in the ONS vignettes), or mark the
years as shocks so that the trend is estimated without them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prep <- mt_prep(step_shocks(2020:2022, action = "interpolate"))
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), data, prep = prep)
```

Whether mortality returns to the pre-pandemic trend is an assumption the
model does not test.

## Coherence

### How do I get forecasts that add up over regions, sexes or causes?

Describe the structure with `mt_hierarchy()` and either model the bottom
strata and sum them (`mt_reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up")`), or model
every node and reconcile the draws (`method = "wls"`, `"mint"`, ...).
Totals that are not in the data are added by `mt_aggregate_strata()`.
Reconciliation of deaths uses exposures of the forecast years; supply
population projections as `exposure` when they are available. See
"Coherent forecasts by sex, region and deprivation" and "Causes of death by
deprivation".

### Will the gap between regions or deprivation groups keep growing?

That depends on the model, not only on the data. Separate models per
stratum extrapolate each stratum's trend, so gaps can widen without bound.
`li_lee()` and `product_ratio()` let strata deviate from a common trend
only through stationary processes, so gaps return towards their past
average. Backtests over a few years rarely separate the two; the choice
is an assumption to state.

## Practicalities

### Are forecasts reproducible?

Yes, with a `seed` (`mt_forecast(..., seed = 1)`, `mt_backtest(..., seed =
1)`). Parallel code uses L'Ecuyer random-number streams.

### How long does it take?

Lee-Carter, Li-Lee and random walks fit in seconds even for hundreds of
strata. One-dimensional PCLM ungrouping takes about two seconds per stratum
for 30 years of single ages; the two-dimensional version is much slower.
`apc_bayes()` runs MCMC chains: with `mcmc_control("fast")` from about
ten seconds (8 age groups, 10 years) to one or two minutes per stratum (19
age groups, 14 years).

### Where do the validation numbers come from?

The `validation/` directory of the source repository runs benchmarks with
thresholds on every change (ungrouping accuracy, interval calibration,
coherence); `dev/calibration.md` documents the interval calibration study.
